title: Beer, and no rice
note: Fictional patient. Values are illustrative and follow the module’s house standard; volumes and concentrations come from the guideline and the unit protocol, not this case. The attending nephrologist’s judgment comes first.

monitor.neuro: Vomiting; very drowsy, rousable to voice

intro:
You are the internal medicine resident on duty at a government hospital in Bulacan. At 23:00 on Friday, the intern, Dr. Joy Bernardo, calls from the emergency room about Mr. Ernesto “Boy” Dela Cruz, 52, a tricycle driver who weighs 54 kg. His wife says that for three weeks he has eaten almost nothing, “not even rice,” while drinking eight to ten bottles of beer a day. Since the afternoon he has vomited several times, and now he is very drowsy, though he opens his eyes to his name.

His sodium is 113 mmol/L, potassium 2.8 mmol/L, glucose 92 mg/dL and serum osmolality 238 mOsm/kg. His blood pressure is 118/76 mm Hg. He takes no regular medicines. Urine osmolality and sodium have been sent. The nephrology fellow on call is Dr. Rafael Cortez.

choices.text: One liter of 0.9% saline over an hour; heavy drinkers are usually dry.
choices.feedback: Vomiting and deep somnolence are severe symptoms, and isotonic saline raises the sodium too slowly and unpredictably to treat them. In a low-solute patient it can also trigger a large water diuresis later.
choices.then: You change the order to hypertonic saline boluses per protocol. After two, at 00:30, his sodium is 118 mmol/L and he is more awake.

choices.text: Wait for the urine osmolality and sodium so that you treat the right disorder.
choices.feedback: Classification matters, but not in the first hour of severe symptoms. The brain is swollen now, and the urine results will not change the emergency treatment.
choices.then: At 23:40 he vomits again and is harder to rouse. You start hypertonic saline boluses per protocol; at 00:30 his sodium is 118 mmol/L.

choices.text: Call the attending, move him to a monitored bed, and give hypertonic saline boluses per protocol.
choices.feedback: Severe symptoms mean cerebral edema now, and a small, quick rise shrinks the brain. The European guideline recommends prompt hypertonic saline (1D), aiming for a 5 mmol/L rise (2D); then the emergency phase stops. Check sodium after each bolus, aiming for a rise of about 5 mmol/L, per the guideline and unit protocol.
choices.then: After two boluses, at 00:30, his sodium is 118 mmol/L and he is more awake. The boluses stop.

choices.text: Fluid restriction for now, and a repeat sodium in the morning to see which way it is going.
choices.feedback: Vomiting and deep somnolence are severe symptoms. Waiting risks seizures and worsening brain swelling, and fluid restriction works far too slowly.
choices.then: At 23:30 the nurse calls: he is barely rousable. You start hypertonic saline boluses per protocol; at 00:30 his sodium is 118 mmol/L.

n2.scene: The urine studies return: urine osmolality 72 mOsm/kg, urine sodium below 10 mmol/L.

choices.text: The syndrome of inappropriate antidiuresis (SIAD): fluid restriction and a vasopressin receptor antagonist.
choices.feedback: SIAD needs a urine osmolality above 100 mOsm/kg; his is 72, so antidiuretic hormone (ADH) is suppressed. The European guideline also recommends against vasopressin receptor antagonists in moderate and profound hyponatremia (1C).
choices.then: Dr. Cortez points to the urine osmolality. You reclassify it as low-solute hyponatremia.

choices.text: Low-solute hyponatremia (beer potomania): too little solute to excrete the water.
choices.feedback: A urine osmolality of 100 mOsm/kg or less means ADH is not acting. The daily solute load sets the most water the kidney can excrete; on beer and no food it is only a few liters. The danger ahead is the water diuresis that comes once solute arrives. ADH is suppressed, but with so little solute he cannot excrete the water he drinks.

choices.text: Pseudohyponatremia: repeat the sodium with a lipid profile before treating anything.
choices.feedback: A reasonable first check in general, but his measured serum osmolality is 238 mOsm/kg, so the hyponatremia is truly hypotonic. Move on to the urine.
choices.then: You reread the urine osmolality and classify it as low-solute hyponatremia.

choices.text: Hypovolemia from vomiting: saline until the sodium is normal.
choices.feedback: Low effective volume releases ADH, and the urine osmolality would be above 100 mOsm/kg; his is 72. “Until normal” also has no ceiling.

n3.scene: His potassium of 2.8 mmol/L needs replacing. His wife asks whether he can eat now, and the nurse asks for the written order.

choices.text: A ceiling of 10 mmol/L over the next 24 hours, counted from now, with sodium checks every six hours.
choices.feedback: The window runs from the first sodium, 113 mmol/L at 23:00, not from now. He has already used 5 mmol/L of it, and with three high-risk features the attending will likely want a lower goal.
choices.then: You rewrite it from 23:00 and call the attending for the goal.

vitals.order: Ceiling ≤123 by Sat 23:00; lower goal per attending; hourly urine

choices.text: Full diet and saline maintenance tonight, to give his kidneys the solute they need.
choices.feedback: Solute is exactly what turns on the water diuresis. Beer potomania, hypokalemia and malnutrition make him high risk for osmotic demyelination, and an uncontrolled rise is the main danger now.
choices.then: Dr. Cortez stops the saline. You write the ceiling from 23:00 and call the attending.

vitals.order: Ceiling ≤123 by Sat 23:00; lower goal per attending; hourly urine

choices.text: From the first sodium: no higher than 123 by 23:00 Saturday, with close checks.
choices.feedback: The house limit is 10 mmol/L in the first 24 hours, measured from the first sodium. For high-risk patients the United States panel suggests lower goals. Potassium entering cells pulls sodium out, so its repletion raises the sodium too. A lower goal set by the attending for a high-risk patient; hourly urine output, frequent sodium checks per protocol, and a note that potassium and food will raise the sodium.

vitals.order: Ceiling ≤123 by Sat 23:00; lower goal per attending; hourly urine

choices.text: No written ceiling: 118 is still low, so faster correction is safer than leaving him there.
choices.feedback: The 2025 meta-analysis linking faster correction with fewer deaths was observational and confounded by illness severity; it does not show that crossing the limit is safe. Osmotic demyelination is irreversible.
choices.then: You write the ceiling from 23:00 and call the attending.

vitals.order: Ceiling ≤123 by Sat 23:00; lower goal per attending; hourly urine

n4.scene: Dr. Bernardo calls at 05:00. His sodium is 122 mmol/L, a rise of 9 mmol/L in six hours, and he has passed 1.4 liters of dilute urine since 01:00. He is alert and hungry.

choices.text: Stop the saline, recheck in two hours, and call if the sodium passes 123.
choices.feedback: The call trigger has already been met: a rise of 8 mmol/L or more within the first 24 hours. With dilute urine flowing, the sodium will cross the ceiling before the recheck.
choices.then: You call Dr. Cortez now. The attending orders re-lowering with desmopressin and electrolyte-free water under close monitoring.

choices.text: He is awake and eating; continue the plan, since he has no symptoms of overcorrection.
choices.feedback: Looking well says nothing about osmotic demyelination, which appears days later. He has nearly used his 24-hour limit in six hours, and the water diuresis is still running.
choices.then: The nurse insists you call. The attending orders re-lowering with desmopressin and electrolyte-free water.

choices.text: Stop the saline and recheck the sodium at 08:00 rounds.
choices.feedback: Stopping the saline is not enough: the dilute urine keeps raising the sodium. A three-hour gap at this rate lets it cross the limit.
choices.then: At 06:00 you call Dr. Cortez. The attending orders re-lowering with desmopressin and electrolyte-free water.

choices.text: Stop all sodium-raising treatment and call the fellow and attending now.
choices.feedback: A sudden flow of dilute urine means the sodium is about to cross the ceiling. The European guideline recommends prompt intervention to re-lower the sodium (1D) with expert input; re-lowering is an attending decision. The attending decides on re-lowering with electrolyte-free water and desmopressin under close monitoring.

n5.scene: At 23:00 on Saturday, 24 hours after the first sodium, he is at 120 mmol/L, a rise of 7. He is eating. His wife asks whether his brain is “safe now.”
n5.prompt: What do you write, and what do you tell her?

choices.text: A ceiling of 8 mmol/L for the next 24 hours, continued checks, and what to watch for.
choices.feedback: The house limit is 8 mmol/L in each 24 hours after the first, until 130 mmol/L. Osmotic demyelination, if it occurs, appears days later, so the family and the team must know its signs. No higher than 128 by Sunday 23:00; continued urine and sodium watch; check for new swallowing difficulty, weakness or altered behavior in the coming days, and explain to her what to watch for and why.

vitals.order: Day 2 ceiling ≤128 by Sun 23:00; late-sign watch

choices.text: The same plan as yesterday: a ceiling of 10 mmol/L for the next 24 hours, with the same checks.
choices.feedback: Close, but the second-day limit is lower: 8 mmol/L in each 24 hours after the first. His risk features have not changed.
choices.then: You correct the ceiling to 8 mmol/L and add the late-sign watch.

vitals.order: Day 2 ceiling ≤128 by Sun 23:00; late-sign watch

choices.text: He is awake and eating; correct freely to normal and stop the checks.
choices.feedback: The limit applies each day until the sodium reaches 130 mmol/L. Meals now supply solute, so the risk of another water diuresis is real.
choices.then: You write the 8 mmol/L ceiling and keep the checks.

vitals.order: Day 2 ceiling ≤128 by Sun 23:00; late-sign watch

end.title: Day 5
end.text: By day 5 Mr. Dela Cruz’s sodium is 131 mmol/L, and he talks, swallows and walks normally. The note records the timeline, the overcorrection at 05:00 and its rescue, and the cause: three weeks of beer with almost no food. His wife learns that meals, not beer, give his kidneys the solute they need to clear water, and the team arranges follow-up for his drinking before discharge.

debrief:
What this case teaches

  • Severe symptoms first: hypertonic boluses aiming for a rise of about 5 mmol/L, then stop.
  • Read the urine osmolality. At 100 mOsm/kg or less, ADH is suppressed; in a beer drinker who does not eat, that means low-solute hyponatremia.
  • Count the ceiling from the first sodium: 10 mmol/L in the first 24 hours and 8 in each 24 hours after, lower when the attending judges the risk high.
  • Watch the urine more closely than the drip. Food, potassium and saline turn on the water diuresis; call at once when dilute urine starts to flow.

See Water physiology, Classify, Severe symptoms and Overcorrection.
